learn.hook: Will the toss go your way before the cricket match? Probability puts a number on your chances!
points: An experiment has outcomes; an event is a collection of outcomes. Outcomes are equally likely if none is favoured over another.
Theoretical probability: P(E) = (number of outcomes favourable to E) / (total number of possible outcomes), when outcomes are equally likely.
0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. A sure event has probability 1 and an impossible event has probability 0.
P(E) + P(not E) = 1, so P(not E) = 1 − P(E). E and 'not E' are complementary events.
The probabilities of all the elementary events of an experiment add up to 1.

example.q: A box has 4 kaju katlis and 6 laddoos. Joseph picks one without looking. What is the probability that it is a laddoo?

learn.reallife: Weather apps, lucky draws at Diwali melas and cricket win predictors all use probability.

games.title: How likely is it?
items: Getting a number less than 7 on a normal die
Getting a head when tossing a coin
Drawing a red card from a full deck
Getting an even number on a die
Picking a vowel from the letters A, E, I, O, U

games.title: Probability facts
items: The probability of an event can be 1.2.
Either E happens or it doesn't, so together they cover every outcome.
A probability can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.
1/4, 0.25 and 25% all mean the same chance.
On a fair coin, getting a head and getting a tail are equally likely.

quiz.q: Which of these can NOT be the probability of an event?
quiz.explain: Probability is always between 0 and 1. A negative value like −0.2 is impossible.
quiz.mistake: Thinks percentages cannot be probabilities

quiz.q: If P(E) = 0.08, what is P(not E)?
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of subtracting from 1

quiz.q: A Diwali gift box has 5 laddoos, 3 barfis and 2 pedas. Aisha picks one without looking. What is P(barfi)?
quiz.explain: There are 10 sweets and 3 are barfis, so P(barfi) = 3/10.
quiz.mistake: Divides by the number of non-barfis (7) instead of the total

quiz.q: What is the probability of a sure event?
quiz.explain: A sure event happens in every outcome, so P = total/total = 1.
quiz.mistake: Confuses sure events with impossible ones

quiz.q: Riya says: 'Either it will rain tomorrow or it won't, so P(rain) = 1/2.' What is wrong with her reasoning?
options: The two outcomes are not equally likely
quiz.explain: P = favourable/total only works when outcomes are equally likely. Rain and no rain usually are not.
quiz.mistake: Uses the formula without checking that outcomes are equally likely

quiz.q: A spinner has 8 equal sectors numbered 1 to 8. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 5?
quiz.explain: Numbers greater than 5 are 6, 7, 8. So P = 3/8.
quiz.mistake: Includes 5 itself, or counts the numbers up to 5

quiz.q: 200 tickets are sold for a lucky draw and Joseph buys 5. What is the probability that he wins the single prize?
quiz.mistake: Counts only one ticket (1/200) or divides by the number of tickets he bought (1/5)

quiz.q: Which pair of outcomes is equally likely?
options: Getting 1 or getting 6 on a fair die
Getting an even number or a number less than 2 on a die
Picking a girl or a boy from a class of 30 girls and 10 boys
A well-prepared student passing or failing
quiz.explain: On a fair die each face has probability 1/6, so 1 and 6 are equally likely. The others have different chances.
quiz.mistake: Assumes any two outcomes are equally likely

teach.ask: Gappu is going to toss a coin: 'How do I work out the probability of getting a head?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes, when all are equally likely. Heads it is!
teach.nudge: What do I count on the top, what on the bottom, and when does this rule work?

learn.hook: One die, two dice, three coins — list every outcome and the probabilities fall into your lap!
points: One coin: 2 outcomes {H, T}. Two coins: 4 outcomes {HH, HT, TH, TT}. Three coins: 8 outcomes.
Two dice: 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes, written as pairs like (2, 5). (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different outcomes.
Always list the sample space first, then count the favourable outcomes.
Watch out: 'two heads, one head, no head' are NOT equally likely outcomes for two coins.

example.q: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum is 8?

learn.reallife: Ludo and Snakes and Ladders players can work out the chance of rolling exactly what they need.

items.q: Two coins: P(at least one head)
Two dice: total number of outcomes
Three coins: total number of outcomes

quiz.q: A die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a prime number?
quiz.explain: The primes on a die are 2, 3 and 5. P = 3/6 = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Counts 1 as a prime and gets 4/6 = 2/3

quiz.q: Two coins are tossed together. What is the probability of getting exactly one head?
quiz.explain: Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. Exactly one head: HT and TH, so P = 2/4 = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Treats 'two heads, one head, no head' as 3 equally likely outcomes (1/3)

quiz.q: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability of a doublet (both dice show the same number)?
quiz.mistake: Counts only one doublet and gets 1/36

quiz.q: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum is 9?
quiz.mistake: Uses the 11 possible sums as equally likely outcomes (4/11)

quiz.q: A die is rolled. What is the probability of NOT getting a multiple of 3?
quiz.explain: Multiples of 3 are 3 and 6, so P(multiple of 3) = 2/6 = 1/3. P(not) = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3.
quiz.mistake: Gives the probability of getting a multiple of 3

quiz.q: Three coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting at least two heads?
quiz.explain: Outcomes with at least 2 heads: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH — 4 of the 8 outcomes. P = 4/8 = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Counts exactly two heads only (3/8) and forgets HHH

quiz.q: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum is greater than 10?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that (5, 6) and (6, 5) are different outcomes

quiz.q: Harpreet and Arjun toss two coins. Harpreet wins if both coins match; Arjun wins if they are different. Is the game fair?
quiz.explain: Match: HH, TT (2 outcomes). Different: HT, TH (2 outcomes). Each has probability 2/4 = 1/2, so the game is fair.
quiz.mistake: Counts HT and TH as one outcome

teach.ask: Gappu throws two dice: 'How many outcomes are there, and how do I find the chance of a sum of 7?'
teach.praise: Tweet! 36 pairs in all, count the ones that work, then divide. I'm a dice master now!
teach.nudge: How many outcomes do two dice have, and how do I count the ones I want?

learn.hook: Shuffle a deck, dip into a bag of marbles, pick a lucky token — the same simple rule works every time!
points: A deck has 52 cards in 4 suits of 13: spades ♠ and clubs ♣ are black, hearts ♥ and diamonds ♦ are red.
Each suit has an ace, 2 to 10, and three face cards — jack, queen and king. So there are 12 face cards and 4 aces.
For bags of balls or marbles, total outcomes = total number of balls.
If some cards or balls are removed, recount the total AND the favourable outcomes.
Use P(not E) = 1 − P(E) when 'not' is easier to count.

example.q: One card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52. What is the probability that it is a face card?
steps: Face cards: jack, queen, king in each of 4 suits = 12

learn.reallife: Card games at family gatherings, lucky-dip stalls and quality checks in factories all use these ideas.

items.text: The number of face cards in a deck is ___
The number of red cards in a deck is ___
The number of black kings in a deck is ___

games.title: Card check
items: An ace is a face card.
Face cards are only the jack, queen and king.
Hearts and diamonds are black suits.
There is only one king of spades: P = 1/52.

quiz.q: A card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. What is the probability of a red face card?
quiz.explain: Red face cards: J, Q, K of hearts and of diamonds = 6. P = 6/52 = 3/26.
quiz.mistake: Counts all 12 face cards (3/13)

quiz.q: A bag has 3 red, 5 white and 4 green marbles. One is drawn at random. What is P(not green)?
quiz.explain: Total = 12 and not green = 8. P = 8/12 = 2/3.
quiz.mistake: Gives P(green) = 4/12 = 1/3

quiz.q: All four aces are removed from a deck of 52 cards. One card is drawn from the rest. What is P(king)?
quiz.explain: 48 cards are left, and all 4 kings are still there. P = 4/48 = 1/12.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to reduce the total from 52 to 48

quiz.q: A box of 100 bulbs has 8 defective ones. One bulb is picked at random. What is the probability that it is good?
quiz.explain: Good bulbs = 92, so P = 92/100 = 23/25.
quiz.mistake: Gives the probability of a defective bulb, or uses the wrong total

quiz.q: A jar at the school fete has tokens numbered 1 to 50. One is drawn. What is the probability that it shows a perfect square?
quiz.explain: Perfect squares up to 50: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49 — that is 7. P = 7/50.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 1 is a perfect square (6/50)

quiz.q: A card is drawn from a deck of 52. What is the probability that it is a black card but not a king?
quiz.explain: There are 26 black cards, including 2 black kings. 26 − 2 = 24, so P = 24/52 = 6/13.
quiz.mistake: Removes all 4 kings instead of only the 2 black ones (11/26)

quiz.q: Meena's bag has 5 blue balls and P(blue) = 1/4. How many balls are in the bag?
quiz.explain: 5/total = 1/4, so total = 5 × 4 = 20.
quiz.mistake: Adds 5 and 4 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: A bag has 5 red balls and some blue balls. P(blue) is twice P(red). How many blue balls are there?
quiz.explain: With the same total, P(blue) = 2 × P(red) means blue balls = 2 × red balls = 10.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the total instead of the number of red balls

teach.ask: Gappu holds a deck of cards: 'What is the chance of drawing a king, and how do I know?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! 4 kings out of 52 cards — that's 1/13. Card shark Gappu!
teach.nudge: How many cards are there in all, and how many of them are kings?
